title: The Case for a Boring Tech Stack
summary: Boring tech is tech whose failure modes you already know. Why that helps on-call, hiring and maintenance, how to spend innovation tokens, and when boring turns into debt.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
It's 9:40, twenty minutes before a release, and the error rate on one endpoint ticks up. Nobody panics. One person opens the logs, another pulls up the slow-query graph, and a third remembers that this exact Postgres warning showed up last spring after an index change. By 9:55 they've agreed on a one-line fix, and the release goes out on time. Nobody will mention that morning at an all-hands.

That's the case for a boring tech stack in one scene. The tools weren't impressive. They were familiar enough that three people could read the same signals and land on the same answer fast. This post covers why that's worth more than it looks, where it stops being true, and how to tell when something new has earned its spot.

Boring means you know how it breaks

The phrase comes from Dan McKinley's 2015 essay Choose Boring Technology, written after his years at Etsy. His definition is precise: boring technology is well understood, both in what it can do and in how it fails. He's careful to say that boring doesn't mean bad. His examples were MySQL, Postgres, PHP, Python, Memcached and cron.

McKinley splits the risk into known unknowns and unknown unknowns. Old tools still surprise you, but you can usually name the gaps ahead of time: "we don't know what happens when the database hits 100% CPU." With shiny new tools, he argues, the pile of failures nobody saw coming is much bigger. Postgres started as a Berkeley research project in 1986 and has nearly 40 years of active development behind it. Almost every strange error it can throw already has a mailing-list thread, a Stack Overflow answer or a teammate who has hit it before.

That history pays off at the worst possible hour. When production slows down at midnight, the on-call engineer on a familiar stack starts with familiar questions: which query changed, which queue is backing up, which deploy touched this path, which metric moved first. None of those questions is clever. They're fast, and fast is what you want at midnight.

More people can help

A popular stack comes with a big pool of people who already know it. In the 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 48.7% of respondents reported using PostgreSQL and 62.3% reported using JavaScript. A new hire who already knows the tools can ship something real in their first week.

Hiring is only half of it. Familiar tools make the whole team sturdier. A junior engineer can paste an error message into a search bar and find ten useful answers. A reviewer can focus on business logic instead of learning a framework's philosophy inside a pull request. A partner team can pitch in without someone translating for them. And when the one person who understands the unusual piece goes on leave, the system doesn't go on leave with them.

The bill arrives after launch

Writing the first version is the cheap part. McKinley's sharpest point is that every new technology brings baggage: someone has to monitor it, write tests around it, learn it well enough to debug it and keep it upgraded. He argues that the long-term cost of keeping a system running reliably far outweighs whatever you save by using a nicer tool on day one.

You feel that cost in the fifth version of a product, after the requirements have changed twice and half the original team has moved on. Upgrading dependencies, reading old code, adding tests, finding examples, explaining a decision to someone who wasn't there: none of it is glamorous, and all of it is cheaper on a stack lots of people understand. The same thinking applies one level up, to service boundaries, in Choosing Boring Boundaries on Purpose.

Spend your novelty on purpose

None of this means you should never adopt anything new. McKinley's model is innovation tokens: a company gets about three, and the supply stays fixed for a long while. Each new database, language or orchestration layer spends one. That makes the real question sharper: is this where we want to spend one of our three?

A good answer usually points at whatever makes your product different. If your edge is real-time collaboration, a new sync engine might be worth a token. If your edge is the product's features, your job queue probably shouldn't be the experimental part. McKinley's process for the decision fits on an index card:

  • Ask how you'd solve the problem with the tools you already run.
  • Write down exactly what makes that too hard. If you can't write it down, you don't have a reason yet.
  • Make adding a technology a decision the whole team talks through, so it doesn't become one person's side quest.
  • If the new tool replaces an old one, commit to migrating the old functionality too. Otherwise you end up running both for years.

When boring turns into debt

Boring has its own failure mode. A team can hide behind comfort and call it prudence. Some old choices carry real costs: a runtime that no longer gets security patches, performance that no longer fits the workload, an ecosystem that's drying up. One test helps: is this tool boring because everyone understands it and it keeps working, or because nobody dares to touch it? The first is a strength. The second is technical debt keeping a straight face, and paying it down is a skill of its own (more on that in Working With Legacy Code).

So the choice comes down to how much surprise you can afford. Every tool makes you pay for learning, hiring, debugging, operating and changing it later. Sometimes a new tool removes a real bottleneck and earns every bit of that. Sometimes the cost hides in onboarding, late-night incidents, thin docs and one expert who can never take a long holiday.

Try this week

  • List every distinct technology your service runs in production. Count how many of them each person on the team could debug at 2 a.m.
  • Find the one only a single person understands, and pair someone else on its next change.
  • Before your next "let's try X" proposal, write McKinley's paragraph: how you'd solve it with what you have, and why that's too hard.
  • If you replaced a tool last year and the old one is still running, put its removal on the roadmap.

faqs.q: What is a boring tech stack?
faqs.a: A stack built from tools whose capabilities and failure modes are well understood. Dan McKinley's examples were MySQL, Postgres, PHP, Python, Memcached and cron. Boring describes how predictable a tool is. It says nothing bad about its quality.

It's Dan McKinley's model for adopting new technology. A company can afford about three new technologies at a time, and that supply stays fixed for a long while. Spend them on the parts that make your product different.

faqs.q: When should a team adopt a new technology?
faqs.a: When you can write down why the tools you already run make the problem too hard, the whole team has talked it through, and you commit to migrating the old functionality off whatever the new tool replaces.

faqs.q: Can a boring stack become a risk?
faqs.a: Yes. If a tool is boring because nobody dares to touch it, with an unsupported runtime, missing security patches or a workload it no longer fits, it has become technical debt and needs a plan to pay it down.
